summary: Registers and documents the haptics top-level media type, under which subtypes for representing haptic data can be registered. It also registers several subtypes that reflect existing practice.

eli5.summary: Haptics is the feel of touch, like a phone buzzing. This creates an official file type family for describing those buzzes and touches.

subtitle: Touch gets its own top-level media type, next to audio and video, with three first haptic formats.

tldr.problem: Haptic data, the instructions that make a device vibrate or push back, had no registered home among Internet media types, and no top-level type fit it well.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9695 registers 'haptics' as a top-level media type under the process in RFC 9694, says unknown subtypes should be treated as 'application/octet-stream', and registers three subtypes: 'ivs', 'hjif' and 'hmpg'.
tldr.outcome: Haptic formats can now be registered as 'haptics' followed by a subtype name. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9993.

today: RFC 9695 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025, and it has been updated by RFC 9993. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What Haptics Is and Why a New Type
sections.content:
Haptics means generating touch-related sensations in a device or interface. The RFC points to typing on a virtual keyboard on a phone as the most common use. Unlike audio and video, haptics needs some form of actuation: small vibrating motors in phones and game controllers, or specialized piezoelectric materials in large touchscreens in vehicles.

Internet media types (RFC 6838) label content carried over Internet protocols. RFC 9695 defines a new top-level type, haptics, following the guidelines in RFC 9694. The type signals that the content specifies haptic data. Specific representation formats are registered beneath it.
sections.eli5: Some things on your phone make it buzz when you tap. This RFC gives the family of buzz files its own name tag, the way pictures and songs already have theirs.

sections.title: The Case for a Top-Level Type
sections.content:
The RFC argues from several directions. Haptic tracks can be played in sync with audio and video, and haptics became part of ISO/IEC 14496-12 (ISOBMFF), 7th Edition, published in January 2022. The text says a strong case can be made for adding haptics to the top-level types the IETF recognizes.

Haptics also has several sub-modalities: vibrotactile, kinesthetic (force feedback), surface (friction), spatial non-contact (ultrasound) and thermal (temperature). Putting haptics under another top-level type would make it harder to define formats for these in a streamlined way.

Finally, the RFC explains why application does not fit. That type has historically been used for code and is treated with great care for security. Haptic data is not code, just as audio and video are not, and it is a property of a media stream rather than an application.

For MP4 files the RFC envisions haptics/mp4 for files with only haptic tracks, video/mp4 for files with video, audio and haptics, and audio/mp4 for audio with haptics.
sections.eli5: Sound is for ears and video is for eyes, so touch deserves its own label too. Filing buzz files under "programs" would be wrong, because they are not programs.

sections.title: Formats Already in Use
sections.content:
The RFC lists existing haptic formats that would live under the new type, noting that these subtypes have not been standardized yet. They include ahap (Apple's AHAP format, the standard encoding on iOS devices), an ogg extension introduced by Google in Android 11, ivs (used in some LG and ASUS phones) and hapt (a vendor-specific format).

It also cites device sales figures from 2023 as evidence that haptics is a common feature of consumer electronics, and expects haptic media to be commonly exchanged between such devices. Of the formats it expects to register later, hmpg and hjif come from ISO/IEC 23090-31, and other candidates, including one under IEEE 1918.1.1, still have no final format name.
sections.eli5: Lots of phones and game gadgets already have their own kinds of buzz files. A shared family name helps them swap files without confusion.

sections.title: Registration and Handling Rules
sections.content:
IANA registered haptics in the Top-Level Media Types registry defined by RFC 9694, and added it as an alternative value of "Type Name" in the media type registration form.

The top-level type says the content needs a haptics subsystem, such as low-level haptics APIs and hardware like one or more actuators. It gives no information about the data format; the subtype names that. Unrecognized subtypes should be treated as application/octet-stream, although implementations may still pass them to the haptics subsystem.

New formats are requested with the media type application form, consulting RFC 6838, and the specification should preferably be freely available. If an implementation does not recognize a parameter sub-value in a comma-separated list, it should ignore it and continue with the others.
sections.eli5: If your device does not know a particular kind of buzz file, it treats it like a mystery package. It may still try to play it on its buzzer.

sections.title: The Three Initial Subtypes
sections.content:
Three subtypes are registered, and they also serve as examples for future registrations. Each lists the contact as Yeshwant Muthusamy and the change controller as ISO/IEC JTC1/SC 29/WG 7 (MPEG 3D Graphics and Haptic Coding).

  • haptics/ivs: a device-independent haptic effect coding based on XML, file extension .ivs. Not all devices may be able to render all effects in an IVS file.
  • haptics/hjif: a human-readable haptic effect coding based on JSON, an interchange format for temporal and spatial haptic effects, extension .hjif.
  • haptics/hmpg: a streamable binary haptic effect coding, extension .hmpg, with encoding considerations of simply binary.

For ivs and hjif the encoding is 8bit if UTF-8 and binary if UTF-16 or UTF-32. HJIF and HMPG effects may target specific parts of the human body and may be tied to a reference device description so rendering software can adapt them to available hardware.
sections.eli5: There are three starter kinds of buzz file: one written in a tag language, one written in a readable list format, and one packed into bytes for fast streaming.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Haptic data is interpreted: it can be signal data and/or descriptive text in XML or JSON. Signal data is typically not executed by endpoint processors and represents minimal security risk. The security profile is expected to be largely consistent with that of visual and audio media.

Descriptive encodings carry more risk. Media rendering is normally implemented with a mix of user and kernel space execution, so in theory malicious instructions in descriptive haptic media could execute arbitrary code in kernel space and bypass permissions or sandboxes. Operating system and device driver implementors should make sure the rendering path is not an attack surface.

Thermal devices (heat) and kinesthetic devices (force feedback) could potentially injure users if heat or force is not properly controlled or exceeds safety levels. Implementors need to take adequate measures to prevent that.

These considerations apply to the registered subtypes and to all future haptics registrations.
sections.eli5: A buzz file should only make a gadget buzz. Builders must make sure a sneaky file cannot trick the gadget into doing other things, or get too hot or push too hard.
